items.a: Hi. I'm Thanh, Albert to friends. Ask me anything, or pick a question below.
Thanh Nguyen. Software engineer, systems by day, small tools at night. I like understanding things from the ground up and then making something that runs.
Thanh is my given name. Albert is the one I use when Thanh is hard to say. traceformula is the handle I have had since I started writing code.

Three things. A write-up of cube algebra, the algebra of 3-tensors built the way matrix algebra is built. Piano practice tools that adapt to what you get wrong. And this site: what should a personal page expose once AI agents visit as often as people do?

Matrix algebra has a natural chip, the multiply-accumulate array. Cube algebra replaces the scalar multiply with a short circular convolution, and the whole theory factors through the Fourier transform into a batch of ordinary matrix algebras. That is the hardware thesis: a transform, then a batch of matmuls.

Yes. The tensor write-up is the clearest example: taking a research literature and assembling it into one development, with proofs at textbook level and the computational primitive visible at every step.

items.q: Tell me about the piano tools
items.a: I started piano as an adult and could not find drills I liked, so I built them: an ear trainer, a note reader, a fingering coach, and 290 tunes to play by ear. Whatever you miss comes back more often. Plain HTML, works offline on a phone.

items.q: Is this site made for AI agents?
items.a: I think a page should say the same thing to a person and to a model fetching raw text. This site has no text on its surface, but it ships about.md, llms.txt, and the exact question bank you are talking to, as qa.json.

Backend systems in Go, C++, Python and Scala at large scale: storage replication, data pipelines, API design, rollouts across regions. Browser-first tools with no framework and no build step. Simulations, interpreters, visualizations. And long-form mathematical writing.

Google, on secure server-side services for YouTube and Search. Amazon, on DynamoDB replication, where a just-in-time log replica cut recovery from 15 minutes to 1. Before that Zocdoc, Uber, and a SaaS startup of my own in Singapore.
B.S. in Computer Science from Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. M.S. in Computer Science from Maharishi University in the United States.

Piano tools, a Python interpreter in JavaScript, a solar system and a constellation sky on Canvas, Conway's Game of Life, a LaTeX renderer, a spaced-repetition app, a knowledge map of two thousand topics, and the cube algebra write-up.
A Python interpreter written in JavaScript. It runs in the browser with nothing to install, and you can share a snippet by link.
I keep the books and courses I have worked through as a force-directed graph instead of a list. About two thousand topics. Clusters appear that I would not have named myself.
Lately: distributed systems patterns, matrix calculus for machine learning, time-series forecasting, graph neural networks, and how large language models are built. The map has the full list.

Distributed systems, linear algebra and tensors, interpreters, LLM agents, quantitative finance, cellular automata, the night sky, piano, spaced repetition, and Mai Hoa Dịch Số, an old Chinese system of divination that I built a calculator for.

items.q: What is Mai Hoa Dịch Số?
items.a: Mai Hoa Dịch Số, the plum-blossom numerology of Shao Yong. You turn a time or a number into a hexagram. I do not use it to decide anything. I like the arithmetic of it.
Two toys for it: a solar system with tilted elliptical orbits and comets, and a starfield that draws constellations as you watch.
Conway's Game of Life with a brush. Draw with the left button, erase with the right, change the brush size, watch it go.
Go, C++, Python, Scala, JavaScript. For my own tools, plain JavaScript with no framework. It still runs in ten years.

items.q: What do you think about AI?
items.a: I use it daily and I build with it. I am less interested in chat and more in what agents do when they become the visitor, the reader, and the caller of everything we build. That question shaped this site.

A six-second video of me, cut into a loop and redrawn live as a few thousand ink dots on a canvas. The chat is a question bank, not a language model, so every answer is mine, word for word. The source is on GitHub.
The face is a real video of me. The voice is a list of answers I wrote, chosen by keyword match. So: real person, scripted mouth.
